title: Calendario Anses: qué prestaciones sociales se cobran en la semana del 21 al 25 de septiembre
content:
Calendario Anses: qué prestaciones sociales se cobran en la semana del 21 al 25 de septiembre
El organismo previsional sigue con la entrega de las jubilaciones, AUH, Asignaciones por Embarazo, entre otras prestaciones
- 3 minutos de lectura'
La Anses (Administración Nacional de Seguridad Social) continúa esta semana con el pago de las prestaciones sociales correspondientes a la semana del 21 al 25 de septiembre, según está establecido en el calendario de pagos.
En la primera del mes se abonan las jubilaciones, AUH, Asignación por Embarazo, Asignación por Prenatal, Pensiones No Contributivas y Asignaciones Familiares de Pensiones No Contributivas.
En el noveno mes del año, las prestaciones sociales tienen un reajuste del 2,11%, en concordancia con la inflación registrada en julio, que fue del 2,1%. Cabe aclarar que para este tipo de actualizaciones, que se hacen mes a mes, se toman los porcentajes de incremento en los precios con dos decimales, y eso arroja el valor exacto actualizado.
El calendario de la Anses en la semana del 21 al 25 de septiembre
Jubilaciones y pensiones que no superen un haber mínimo
- DNI terminados en 9: 21 de septiembre
Jubilaciones y pensiones que superen un haber mínimo
- DNI terminados en 0 y 1: 22 de septiembre
- DNI terminados en 2 y 3: 23 de septiembre
- DNI terminados en 4 y 5: 24 de septiembre
- DNI terminados en 6 y 7: 25 de septiembre
Asignación Universal por Hijo y Asignación Familiar por Hijo
- DNI terminados en 9: 21 de septiembre
Asignación por Embarazo
- DNI terminados en 7: 21 de septiembre
- DNI terminados en 8: 22 de septiembre
- DNI terminados en 9: 23 de septiembre
Asignación por Maternidad
- Se cobra el primer día del calendario de pago para todas las terminaciones de DNI
Asignaciones Pago Único (Matrimonio, Nacimiento, Adopción)
- Todas las terminaciones de documento: 11 de agosto al 11 de septiembre
Asignaciones Familiares de Pensiones No Contributivas
- Todas las terminaciones de documento: 8 de septiembre al 9 de octubre
Cómo saber si tengo que cobrar alguna prestación de la Anses
Las personas que reciben prestaciones sociales a través de la Anses pueden consultar dónde y cuándo tienen el próximo cobro, el cual está determinado por el calendario de pagos que se realiza cada mes.
Para eso, deben seguir los siguientes pasos:
- Ingresar a la página de la Anses
- Completar el formulario con el número de beneficio o de CUIL
- Hacer clic en el botón “Consulta”
- Si corresponde, el sistema informará el lugar y la fecha de cobro (desde el primer día hasta el último en que se puede cobrar la asistencia en cuestión)
Cómo elegir el medio de pago para las prestaciones de la Anses
- Ingresar a Mi Anses o descargar la aplicación, con CUIL y Clave de la Seguridad Social.
- Seleccionar la opción Cobros
- Luego hacer click en la opción Cambiar medio de cobro jubilaciones y pensiones o Cambiar medio de cobro Asignaciones Familiares, según corresponda.
- Corroborar que los datos de contacto (correo electrónico, celular y domicilio) estén actualizados y verificados, lo que puede realizarse en el momento.
- Cargar el código de validación recibido por correo electrónico o SMS y confirmar el DNI, ingresando el correspondiente número de trámite.
- Una vez ingresado dicho código, se podrá optar por el nuevo medio de cobro dentro de las opciones habilitadas.
- En el caso de las asignaciones, podrán consultar el medio de cobro actual y seleccionar el nuevo.
Cabe destacar que quienes residan en zona austral deben optar por una sucursal bancaria para poder mantener el adicional correspondiente a dicha zona.
Para todos los casos, la elección estará vigente a partir de los 60 días de solicitada.

title: Two top performing students talk their aspirations
content: It was around 3 p.m. on Friday, September 11, when Henriette Umukundwa received a phone call from her mother in Ruhango District, telling her that she was among the top performers in the Advanced Level national examination results announced that day. Uwukundwa, 19, was washing dishes at her sister’s home in Kigali, where she had gone to visit. “When I heard that I was among the best performers, I was very surprised. I thought it was a scam. I cried a lot, tears of joy. Then I followed the event of the release of the national exams results on YouTube. That's when I confirmed that it was true,” she told The New Times. ALSO READ: Who are the top performers in A-Level national exams? The former student of ACEJ Karama Technical Secondary School (TSS) topped in Accounting with a score of 95.23 percent. Accounting was among the Professional Education combinations. Umukundwa attributed her performance to hard work, following her teachers’ advice to work in teams and conducting extensive research. “My teachers equipped me with skills, encouraged me to do research and also to enjoy teamwork, saying that ‘one pillar doesn’t make a house’. This helped me feel that I need others as they need me, where we shared knowledge and revised together,” she said. Her favourite subjects were auditing, financial mathematics and management. She studied extensively, took notes and made summaries to improve her understanding, and paid attention during lessons. ALSO READ: 94% of A-Level candidates pass national exams She also prepared a revision timetable, identifying subjects and topics she did not clearly understand and giving them more attention. Her parents were also supportive, she said. They supported her and encouraged her to aim high in life. As a child, Umukundwa wanted to become a doctor, but her interests changed as she grew older and she became more drawn to accounting. She now plans to study accounting at university, gain more knowledge and experience, and work towards becoming a qualified accountant. “The advice I can give to others who want to perform well is to focus on their lessons and manage their time well,” Umukundwa said. “They should pay attention in class, listen to their teachers and make enough time for revision and other schoolwork. Staying focused and using their time well can help them keep up with their studies and improve their performance.” Youssouf Bisangabagabo, the headmaster of ACEJ Karama TSS, said Umukundwa was a class monitress and served as an accountant in the Adventist group. She was always among the top three students in her class and was a responsible student who was useful to the community. In her free time, the youngster enjoys reading history books and catching up with friends. Another top performer, Naomie Umunyurwa Karangwa, was with her parents when the national examination results were announced. Karangwa, 17, sat with her parents to watch the announcement, expecting to see good marks. She knew she had qualified for a diploma but did not know she had performed well enough to emerge as the top performer in the Technical Secondary School category. Karangwa scored 94.74 percent. She studied Craft and Recreational Arts at Ecole d’Arts de Nyundo in Rubavu District. As she and her parents watched the results announcement live on YouTube on September 11, Karangwa was waiting for the link to check her individual results and surprise her family. “Then, as they were reading the names of the best performers, I heard my name. I could hardly believe it,” she recalled in an interview with The New Times. “I was really shocked. I replayed that part of the programme more than five times because I could not believe it could be me. I never thought I could perform that well and take the national top position,” Her parents were equally surprised, and the three cried with joy. The results came after a year in which she relied on her usual study habits, including waking up early, revising notes and taking notes in class. But she said discipline and respect were just as important. Karangwa said respect means recognising that no matter how capable one is, there will always be something they can learn from another person. She said having this sense prevents people from seeing themselves as better than others and allows them to learn from those with abilities they may not have. She credits her parents, teachers and friends, as well as the education she received, for supporting her. “My parents always made sure that I did not lack anything I needed for school. They provided my school fees and the equipment I needed, along with parental advice that showed me the right path to success,” she said. Her teachers also supported her through classwork and practical exercises. “They tried their level best to help me, especially when I struggled. Through classwork and practical exercises, they helped me get back on my feet, develop my skills and realise my potential. Their support pushed me to work harder, and my parents continue to encourage me to pursue my ambitions,” she said. Karangwa wants to specialise in industrial design, mainly architecture and 3D art. She is interested in the detailed designs seen in some historic buildings, including relief sculptures and floral patterns. Karangwa said many modern buildings are look very minimalist and have fewer of these artistic details. She wants to bring some of that detail back into modern architectural design by creating complex designs that tell a story. Her interest in architecture has drawn her to the work of the late Iraqi-British architect Zaha Hadid, whom she considers a role model. Hadid faced years of criticism over her curvaceous, and futuristic designs that were considered too radical or difficult to build, with many of her early projects remaining on paper before more of her designs were realised. Karangwa admires Hadid for continuing to pursue architecture despite the criticism she faced. The youngster advises fellow students to work hard, stay disciplined and take advice seriously, saying pressure should be seen as a privilege because it pushes people to work harder. Of the 108,406 candidates who sat the 2025/26 Advanced Level national examinations, 94.33 percent passed, Girls accounted for 55.05 percent of those who registered.

title: Ethiopia’s Fields Are Becoming a Laboratory for Africa’s Next Agricultural Revolution
content:
Ethiopia’s Fields Are Becoming a Laboratory for Africa’s Next Agricultural Revolution
Addis Ababa, September 21, 2026 (FMC) — Some agricultural transformations are measured in harvests. Others are measured in the number of assumptions they force an entire sector to reconsider.
Across Ethiopia, an increasingly important experiment has been unfolding not inside a single research station or demonstration plot, but across millions of hectares: what happens when improved varieties, irrigation, mechanization, cluster farming, extension systems, climate information and new production practices are taken from the laboratory and pushed toward national scale?
The answer is beginning to reshape the country’s agricultural trajectory—and to attract attention well beyond its borders.
The transformation is particularly visible in wheat. Ethiopia’s rapid expansion of irrigated wheat production brought together several elements that are often treated separately in agricultural development: heat-tolerant varieties, irrigation, improved agronomic practices, organized production, research, extension and market linkages. By 2023, heat-tolerant irrigated wheat production had reached about one million hectares, with average productivity of around four tonnes per hectare, according to research documented through the FAO agricultural knowledge platform. The approach was identified as having potential relevance for wider African food-security efforts.
That is what makes the Ethiopian experience more consequential than a single crop story.
The country has increasingly been using agriculture as a field for systems integration—bringing technologies, institutions and production models together and testing what happens when they operate at scale.
Cluster farming is one such experiment. Rather than leaving millions of smallholders to confront modern agricultural markets and technologies individually, production is increasingly organized around coordinated areas and common production practices. Ethiopia says its cluster-farming system now involves about 9.5 million farmers cultivating 12.8 million hectares, with reported gains in productivity and farmer incomes.
Irrigation represents another major shift.
For generations, much of Ethiopian agriculture has been tied closely to the rhythm of seasonal rainfall. Expanding irrigation changes that equation by allowing farmers to manage water rather than simply wait for it. It can create additional production seasons, diversify crops and reduce exposure to erratic rainfall. The World Bank has identified irrigation as a central pathway for increasing agricultural productivity and strengthening food security in Ethiopia, including through multiple cropping seasons and greater production of diverse and drought-resistant crops.
The significance is not simply that more land is being irrigated.
It is that the production calendar itself can be redesigned.
The same logic extends to seeds. Improved varieties adapted to different agro-ecological conditions—including heat-tolerant wheat—are allowing production systems to move into environments once considered considerably more difficult. Research on Ethiopia’s irrigated wheat expansion has highlighted the role of improved varieties, cluster farming, research institutions, extension services and private-sector actors in bringing these technologies together at scale.
Mechanization adds another layer.
Agricultural modernization cannot be reduced to putting tractors into fields. It involves changing the economics and timing of land preparation, planting, harvesting, threshing, transport and post-harvest handling. Ethiopia’s agricultural development priorities explicitly include expanding mechanization alongside irrigation, horticulture, private-sector participation and institutional capacity.
And increasingly, the experiment is becoming digital.
Weather and climate information, for example, can become a production input in its own right. Research involving Ethiopian farming households found that access to weather and climate services was associated with productivity increases of 27 percent for maize and 17 percent for wheat, underscoring the potential value of information alongside physical inputs such as fertilizer and improved seed.
Taken together, these developments point toward a different understanding of agricultural innovation.
The important question is no longer only whether Ethiopia can produce a better seed, introduce a new machine, expand irrigation or teach a better farming technique. The larger question is whether these components can be assembled into a functioning production system and reproduced at national scale.
That is where Ethiopia’s agricultural experience becomes potentially continental in significance.
Africa does not lack agricultural potential. It has land, water, diverse agro-ecologies, a vast farming population and enormous domestic and regional markets. What has often been missing is the capacity to convert those assets consistently into productivity, reliable supply, commercial value and food-system resilience.
Ethiopia’s ongoing experiment is therefore less about discovering one magical agricultural solution than about testing how several solutions can work together.
Its emerging model is built around a simple but powerful proposition: productivity can be engineered.
Water can be managed. Production seasons can be extended. Varieties can be adapted. Farms can be organized. Information can reach farmers. Machinery can reduce bottlenecks. Research can feed directly into production. Markets can pull output through the value chain.
None of these changes eliminates the country’s agricultural challenges. Ethiopia still faces droughts, floods, pests, conflict-related disruptions, market constraints and serious food-security problems in vulnerable areas. FAO continues to report significant food-security pressures, particularly in pastoral regions affected by climatic and economic shocks.
But precisely because the challenges remain, the scale of the agricultural experiment matters.
Ethiopia is testing whether a predominantly smallholder agricultural economy can progressively move from vulnerability toward greater productivity, diversification and resilience without waiting for every constraint to disappear first.
That makes the Ethiopian countryside something more than the traditional backdrop to a national development story.
It is becoming a living testing ground for African agricultural transformation.
The most consequential harvest may therefore not be measured only in tonnes of wheat, maize, coffee or other crops. It may be measured in knowledge: which technologies work in which environments, which production systems can scale, which institutional arrangements improve farmer productivity, and which combinations can turn Africa’s enormous agricultural potential into dependable food and economic capacity.
If those lessons can travel—from Ethiopia’s irrigated lowlands to other African production zones, from research institutions to farmers, and from individual crops to entire food systems—the experiment taking place in Ethiopian fields could ultimately become part of something much larger.
Not simply an agricultural transformation in one country.
A laboratory for the continent.

title: How the Architecture of Sound Is Transforming Cities
content:
This story is part of The Sonic Commons, a series about the health effects of environmental noise. It is supported by the Nova Institute for Health.
Before Chris Downey lost his sight, he had a wind chime on his front porch. After he became blind, he realized that he could listen out for it to help him find his way home. But after a few years, his nextdoor neighbor added a wind chime to their porch. And then the neighbor on the other side, just uphill, added a chime of their own. “Three in a row!” Downey said.
He assumed at this point that his chime would no longer be able to help him locate his house. But then he noticed that the chime that the neighbor up the hill had hung was slightly higher in pitch compared to his own, and the neighbor who lived slightly downhill had hung lower, deeper chimes. “It was completely coincidental,” Downey said. “But they were perfectly sonified to match the topographic condition.”
Downey had worked as an architect for 20 years before he became blind in 2008, and this chorus of wind chimes suggested a new direction in his work: The sounds of the city weren’t just decorative, musical — they could define the physical contours of a space as dramatically as a concrete wall or an open door to the street.
He began developing a set of design principles that understood architectural accessibility not only in terms of wheelchair ramps and braille on elevator buttons, but ones that considered the ways that sound (and other senses) shaped the experience of blind and other disabled people navigating the built environment. He became part of an evolving conversation in inclusive design that expanded the idea of access, and reconsidered the place of the disabled body in public space. A month after the brain surgery that caused him to lose his vision, he was back at work.
A few years into this new phase of his career, Downey started working with Arup, an engineering consulting firm that had developed an immersive spatial audio lab. Their work allowed Downey to create sonic architectural blueprints by simulating the sound of a space — an atrium, hallway or pavilion — before the design was constructed (after which, Downey pointed out, it would be too late to meaningfully adjust the soundscape). As part of this process, Arup recorded the sound of Downey’s cane tapping on various materials he wanted to use, and placed these recordings within the virtual designs to understand the sonic dimensions of his plans.
Today, Downey is working on a project to combine the campuses of a school for the Deaf and a school for the blind in Indiana. Working with Arup, and collaborating with a Deaf architect, he’s modeling pathways through the campus and painstakingly constructing a useful, pleasurable soundscape for the blind students. “We’re not adding sounds to it,” Downey said. “We’re letting the architectural space and material shape the sound.” As a blind student at the Indiana school makes their way from the locker area to the classrooms, in Downey’s new design, the soundscape will subtly shift from a more open, reverberant space filled with reflective surfaces, to a dampened passage, indicating the location of the classrooms.
Downey applies these same principles to the plans he makes for mainstream projects like museums, offices and transit centers. But making a space accessible for blind and low-vision people often also means thinking beyond sound. The majority of people with visual impairments have some form of light perception, so accessible design for the blind must (perhaps counterintuitively) pay attention to visual considerations as much as sonic and tactile ones. This is why the warning strip that runs along the edges of subway platforms must be bright yellow as well as mottled with discernible bumps.
In urban spaces, sound pollution often prevents travelers from relying on sound alone as a cue. In his design for the Salesforce Transit Center in San Francisco, Downey had to contend with a terminal that held dozens of buses at a time, drowning out any subtle acoustic design he might have been tempted to craft. Likewise, the pattern of bus traffic — swooping in and out of loading bays — created a sawtooth-shaped curb that made for an inefficient landmark for cane travelers. “You couldn’t follow the curb along the edge, otherwise you’ll be there all day, going in and out, in and out,” Downey said. His solution was to mark the route with a series of linear grooves and a textured pathway a cane user could find and follow. “You move from smooth, polished concrete to a rougher surface,” he said. “That’s the signal path to the exit.”
This also had the advantage of integrating blind people into the design. “The yellow, truncated-dome guiding strip, that’s the typical way of thinking,” Downey said. “Yes, it’s needed for a smooth transition from the sidewalk to the road, but putting it down the length of a sidewalk or terminal — nobody benefits except, in theory, the blind person.” Yellow warning strips are normally reserved for hazards, like a subway track, so using them for navigation sends a mixed signal. A solution like the textured concrete pathway, which adds an elegant visual accent along with a tactile guide, Downey said, is “more approachable, and less stigmatizing.”

The notion of universal design — that design for disability leads to better design for everyone — has undeniable appeal (the curb cut, which benefits wheelchair users, but quickly became beloved by people with strollers, carts, scooters, and so on, is the canonical example). But the reality is that building access also creates conflict. Some people who use walkers or wheelchairs, including those with spinal-cord injuries, hate rumble-strips and other textured elements on the ground that blind people value as warning or wayfinding elements. For the concrete in the Salesforce Transit Center, Downey built full-size mockups in the construction yard and brought in people with a variety of mobility impairments, in addition to cane and guide-dog users, to find a texture that was at once discernible to blind people but minimized the discomfort of those who needed to roll over it.
Even within groups of blind and low-vision people, consensus on best practices can be elusive. Paul DeFazio, a blind architect, was consulting on accessible signage in a renovation of Boston’s Logan airport. “They kept making signs with a light-green background and white text,” DeFazio said. “I told them, ‘You need to make the background black. … That’s what’s best for blind people.’ Then, they brought in a group of user testers, one of whom said of the black version: ‘I can’t see that! You have to use a white background!'”
The conflict, for DeFazio, was a sign that the design process was working. “The depoliticized version feels too good,” he said, referring to a situation where, say, a blind person convinces the designers that the black background is the right choice, and everyone agrees, pats each other on the back, and goes home. “That’s consensus.” DeFazio is more interested in dissensus: “I don’t know what’s going to feel good for you,” he said, “but we can create a space and figure it out together.” In the end, DeFazio said, the group may never arrive at an agreement. “Sometimes you just have to be comfortable with the fact that we need different things.”
In her role as principal access and mobility planner at the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency, Maddy Ruvolo deals with lots of disabled dissensus. “So much of transportation planning is about contested use of space,” she said. “And accessibility is a big piece of that.” She described a “dilemma” around parking: Disabled people are statistically more likely to be pedestrians, and use public transit, and so efforts to reduce the presence of cars (and, thus, parking spaces) increase pedestrian safety and the efficiency of public transit. But, Ruvolo said, there are also many people with disabilities who “depend on cars for mobility, and have real concerns about needing to park near their destinations.” As with DeFazio’s dilemma at Logan airport, compromise and friction is a permanent fixture of the landscape.
The rise of hybrid electric vehicles in the early 2000s quieted the soundscape by reducing the number of loud combustion engines. But after a sharp rise in near-misses, injuries and, in some cases, fatalities in encounters between people (many of them blind) and these new, quieter cars, blind groups called for legislation. The Pedestrian Safety Act of 2010 finally established a requirement for all hybrid and electric vehicles to make a discernible sound under 20mph. Downey sees this as an opportunity. “We now have the ability to design an acoustic urban space with better sound,” he said. But not all EV noise is created equal. Downey had strong opinions about the variety of sounds that EVs and hybrids made. When a friend came to pick him up in an Audi e-tron, Downey thought: Now, this is what an EV should sound like. “It didn’t sound apologetic — they weren’t fulfilling a requirement,” he said. “Someone thought: What should it really sound like? It’s an authentic, impressive-sounding, fabricated automotive sound.”
The next arena after EVs is, of course, AVs — autonomous vehicles, from Google’s driverless Waymo taxis on the streets of Phoenix and L.A., to Honolulu’s autonomous metro train system. Many blind people (myself included) are thrilled at the prospect of access to a car that doesn’t rely on someone else’s schedule, sobriety or skill as a driver. But blind (and other disabled) riders sometimes rely on human interaction: Many blind people want to confirm with their driver that their destination is indeed where the map says it is once they’ve arrived. And finding an idling driverless car can be much harder than finding one with a human who might roll down their window and call out your name. After blind organizations petitioned Waymo, riders can now trigger a honk or even a short digital melody to help them find their ride in a noisy environment.
Perhaps the most profound shift in blind people’s experience of navigating urban environments is the rise of the smartphone. “When I’m riding in a car, with the windows rolled up, I’m in a cocoon,” Mike May said. He’s been developing consumer tech to help blind people with navigation for more than 30 years, most recently at the American Printing House for the Blind in Louisville. “You’re 100 percent dependent on the sighted person knowing what’s out there.” But when GPS came on the scene, May saw a new way for a blind person to explore their environment. “There’s a whole world, with millions of points of interest, and I can know what they are,” he said.
The problem is that Google Maps and other mainstream products aren’t verbose enough. “Driving along, the sighted person doesn’t want to hear about everything they’re passing, because they can see it,” May said. But the blind person wants to know about the dog groomer studio tucked into the shadow of the Starbucks, or a new falafel joint in their neighborhood. “Google and Apple don’t announce that info, because sighted people don’t need it,” May said. So he created a series of technological interventions — most recently an app called Indigo — that deliver that higher level of verbosity. May’s app is one of dozens that exist to solve variations on this problem. There are apps that help with street crossings, apps that help plan routes, apps that print tactile maps and apps that aid in indoor navigation. And in the last few years, multimodal A.I. like ChatGPT and Meta’s sunglasses can use front-facing cameras to describe the environment.
“We’re at a tipping point,” Stephanie Enyart, chief public policy and research officer at the American Foundation for the Blind, said. “People are developing apps like wildfire, and there’s an overstimulation effect, from a sonic perspective.” The modern blind person has to keep track of a complex inventory of digital bleeps, alerts, melodies, announcements and chimes, some of which might be trivial and some of which might be offering urgent information about their environment. As with so much A.I. discourse, there is at once tremendous excitement at the affordances it offers (the ability, for example, for a blind person to receive instant, interactive, in-depth descriptions of everything from an airline gate to a museum exhibition), but the risk of hallucination remains real, to say nothing of the serious environmental, social and labor concerns. A flub on a description of a happy-hour menu is frustrating; a mistake on a street crossing could be catastrophic. “The stakes are so high,” Enyart said.
In spite of this extensive range of cutting-edge technological and architectural interventions into the built environment, every blind person I spoke with about urban accessibility mentioned what Bryan Bashin, president of the Be My Eyes Foundation, one of the aforementioned tech solutions, called “inadvertent accessibility.” These are the thousands of small features of the environment that weren’t installed to be helpful, but rather — like the trio of ascending windchimes on Downey’s street — arise naturally, and offer at least as much delight as utility. “Have you ever heard the acoustic signature of a picket fence?” Bashin asked. “Or noticed a particular click and clack in a railroad that denotes an exact spot in a hundred-mile system?”
DeFazio, the blind architect who consulted on the Logan Airport signage, recently explored Harvard’s Science and Engineering Complex while researching a blind architectural curriculum he’s developing. “The building is like the inside of a Dr. Seuss book,” he said. “Big atriums that bounce sound in a disorienting way.” He heard someone playing a piano, but struggled to locate it in the acoustically off-kilter hall, and found the experience of wandering around intensely pleasurable, even as it was also unmistakably “weird and confusing” to navigate.
“People say that accessibility is the foundation of the house,” DeFazio said, referring to basic architectural compliance: Can every visitor enter the building, use the bathroom, and avoid grievous bodily injury along the way? But this narrow focus can be limiting. “A house with just a foundation isn’t going to be very welcoming,” he said. “It feels like we’re never getting to the part that’s above that foundation; the ceiling, the interesting parts” — the strange pleasures of an eccentric soundscape. “It’s time for us to expand what ‘access’ means.”

title: Vet prescription fees capped under rule changes
content:
Vet prescription fees capped under rule changes
- Published
Written prescription fees from vets will be capped at £21 as part of a raft of changes that practices will be legally required to bring in over the coming months.
Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online, write price estimates ahead of treatment, and publish price lists for services as part of the rule updates.
The official competition watchdog has brought the measures into force after its investigation into the sector found prices had been rising at nearly twice the rate of inflation.
However, critics say the measures will hit independent vets hardest and will benefit the six firms that own more than two-thirds of practices.
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) made its remedies for the sector legally binding as of Tuesday and vets have up to 12 months to bring all the changes in.
As well as capping prescription fees, other changes include:
- Vet practices must publish a "comprehensive" price list for standard services – including consultations, common procedures, and cremation options
- A written estimate must be provided in advance for any treatment expected to cost £500 or more, including aftercare costs, plus an itemised bill. Emergencies are the only exception to this
- Vet businesses must make clear whether they are part of a group or an independent business
- To help pet owners compare local practices, price and ownership information will be made available through the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons' "Find a Vet" service, which will share the data with third-party comparison sites.
The timelines for when vets need to bring in the fixes depends on the exact regulation and the group's size. The CMA sets it out here., external
"The changes that are being required are changes that will help inform pet owners about prices," said CMA panel chair Martin Coleman.
However, Cate Titterton, the owner of an independent vet service in Saltburn, told the BBC the changes will make trips to the vets more expensive for customers.
"Veterinary practices still have to have a pharmacy that is fully stocked, so if we're not making that tiny profit on the drugs, we're going to have to make some profit elsewhere.
"So, things like services, consultations, surgeries – unfortunately, those prices are very, very likely to have to go up."
She believes there is "one clear winner" from this - larger vet groups and the corporates.
Cat Henstridge, another vet, said it was "wonderful" that businesses must now make clear if they are part of a large group, but noted that such groups "have not actually been asked to change their ownership of any clinics or anything like that".
Speaking on the Today programme, she advised pet owners who are worried about the cost of care to "be open and honest with your vet about what is affordable for you".
"There is always going to be a bill. Veterinary medicine is private medicine. Owning a pet does come with the responsibility of paying for their care.
"[By] working with us, we can make it work for you, but you have to tell us about it first," she said.
British Veterinary Association President Dr Rob Williams said veterinary practices were already largely working to the CMA's remedies, including the orders relating to complaints handling, price estimates for routine procedures and prescription costs.
"We've been clear with the CMA throughout its investigation that it must ensure its remedies do not disproportionately impact smaller, independent practices and we've pushed back where we've had concerns," Williams said.
Vet surgeries 'not interested in the animal'
One person hoping to see a cheaper more transparent market for vet services is Clive Di Giorgio, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice.
He says he was quoted thousands of pounds for treatment after a vet told him that a rash on his dog Louis' back was "definitely" a sign of cancer.
However, after going to a different vet surgery, he says he was told Louis' rash was not cancerous.
A treatment of steroids, antibiotics, and a spray cleared up the rash in two weeks, Clive says.
"You just don't feel as if when you go to the vets now they're interested in the animal," he says.
"You feel as if all the interest is how much money they can basically squeeze from you."

title: How to combat Punjab’s drugs-in-school menace? Teach the teachers to identify abuse
content:
With the drug addiction and substance use among schoolchildren continuing to be a concern, the teachers in Punjab’s government schools are undergoing a special training to detect such children at an early stage for further treatment and counselling.
The training is being imparted by experts from Dr BR Ambedkar Institute of Medical Sciences (AIMS), Mohali. The training is being conducted under the AAP’s ‘Yuddh Nasheyan Virudh’ campaign.
With Punjab’s drug addiction problem having its roots in the border belt, focus and priority has been given to teachers in border districts. Starting from Amritsar, the training has already been imparted in border districts Fazilka, Tarn Taran and Gurdaspur, while it has also commenced in Pathankot this week.




Speaking to The Indian Express, Dr Balwinder Singh Saini, assistant director, State Council of Educational Research and Training (SCERT), Punjab, said that qualified psychologists from the AIMS, Mohali, along with other experts have been engaged to train teachers. “Teachers are the frontline communicators with children, especially teens, in the classrooms. They are being trained in how they have to handle the situation if they come across any such child whom they might suspect of substance use. They have to help the child, not reprimand, humiliate or scold him/her. We started from border belt, seeing the gravity of the drug problem in these districts; but the entire state will be covered in phases,” he said.
The programme is titled “Teacher Awareness Building Programme for Student Mental Health and Substance Use: Strengthening School Ecosystems in Punjab”. Recognising schools as “critical platforms for prevention and early intervention”, the structured teacher sensitisation programme is being implemented across districts.
“Teachers play a vital role in shaping students’ emotional, behavioural, and social development. However, most teachers lack formal training to recognise early warning signs, often interpreting distress-related behaviours as indiscipline. This underscores the need to reframe substance use as a psychosocial and health concern rather than a moral issue,” says the brief note of the programme prepared by AIMS, Mohali.
During the training, teachers are being sensitized on how to engage with students through private, non-judgmental conversations, identifying early warning signs such as behavioral and emotional changes, referring students to counsellors when necessary, creating emotionally safe and inclusive classroom environments, promoting awareness and preventive discussions on substance use etc.
Story continues below this ad
Survey shows ‘behavioral shift’ in teachers after training
With Amritsar being the first district where the training was imparted, a pilot feedback survey conducted by AIMS has found that majority teachers have found the training to be extremely helpful. The programme reached over 2800 teachers from high and senior secondary schools in Amritsar district.
According to the analysis report submitted to the education department for Amritsar, 76% teachers reported feeling motivated to actively contribute towards building a healthier and more supportive school environment. At least 60% expressed confidence in their ability to appropriately respond to suspected substance use among students. At least 86% teachers acknowledged the link between adolescent substance use and factors such as stress, peer influence, emotional challenges, and adverse social environments, demonstrating a shift towards a psychosocial understanding of substance use.
Among the qualitative outcomes, the trainers observed a shift in behaviour interpretation.
“Teachers reported a significant shift in how they interpret student behaviour. Actions such as aggression, withdrawal, inattentiveness, and irritability previously viewed as indiscipline are now increasingly recognised as potential indicators of emotional distress or vulnerability to substance use. Teachers demonstrated increased awareness of contributing factors such as mental health conditions, peer dynamics, family environment, and neurobiological aspects of addiction. Importantly, there was a clear shift towards a recovery-oriented perspective, with greater emphasis on empathy, support, and the possibility of positive change,” says the report.
Story continues below this ad
With a budget of Rs 4.60 lakh per district, the training is being supported through the funds under the Nasha Mukti Bharat Abhiyan (NMBA) / National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR).
Punjab secretary education Sonali Giri said: “No child will be identified publicly. Training will only help teachers in seeking further help if any such student is detected.”

title: How a teacake tycoon helped to save a village's lifeboat station
content:
How a teacake tycoon helped to save a village's lifeboat station
- Published
A decade ago there was a day of celebration in the little Borders coastal village of St Abbs that they will never forget.
The RNLI closed its lifeboat station in 2015 - bringing a 104-year association to an end - saying there was no clear need for it with one nearby in Eyemouth.
The community rallied round to raise the money needed to bring a boat back and found a surprise ally in the shape of the teacake tycoon Sir Boyd Tunnock.
Just a year later, the Thomas Tunnock lifeboat, named in honour of the businessman's late brother and grandfather, was launched to great acclaim.
- Teacakes toasted at lifeboat launch - Published17 September 2016

- Lifeboat link ends after 104 years - Published8 September 2015

The story of the lifeboat station at St Abbs started with tragedy.
In October 1907 the cargo vessel Alfred Erlandsen struck nearby rocks and the villagers who gathered at the clifftop could only listen to their cries for help.
Accounts vary on how many perished; some say 17 including the captain's wife. The only survivor was his great Dane dog Karo which managed to swim ashore.
One of those who witnessed the shipwreck was women's rights campaigner and philanthropist Jane Hay who wrote to the Edinburgh Evening News:" I write to say that personally I shall never rest content till we have a lifeboat and rocket apparatus of our own in St Abbs."
Four years later, in August 1911, the RNLI established one there - the Helen Smitton - with the dog Karo, which had been involved in fundraising, said to have been among the guests who watched the boat arrive.
Over the course of the next century, the St Abbs lifeboat rescued hundreds of people but in 2015 it found itself in need of saving when the charity announced that, following an "extensive review", the service was to be withdrawn.
Cover from nearby Eyemouth was promised instead, but the plans sparked outcry with a petition against the move gathering about 13,000 signatures.
On 8 September 2015, the station closed - swiftly followed by an appeal to raise the £500,000 needed to fund an independent lifeboat.
That was where businessman Tunnock stepped in with a donation which, he said at the time, amounted to a "lot of caramel wafers".
He agreed to put £250,000 towards the boat and, barely a year after the old station closed, the new boat was officially launched.
Current operations manager, Barry Shaw, said that it had allowed them to carry on a service which was highly valued in the village and beyond.
"We've lost some of our old crew from 10 years ago, unfortunately, but we've got new members," he said.
"But the way the lifeboat operates is just in the same way as we were doing 10 years ago.
"We're still answering the calls from the coastguard and we're protecting the people who use the coast around our area."
He said the donation from Tunnock had allowed them to get the lifeboat "a lot quicker than was anticipated".
"Having a lifeboat still here and still operational, I think it's been a massive achievement from all the volunteers, not just the lifeboat crew," he added.
He said the station remained of huge importance to a "very small village".
"It sits right in the heart of the harbour," he said.
"It is still crewed by local people - our helms are local people.
"We've got a dive boat operator, we've got fishermen - they're still helming our boat.
"They know the water like nobody else."
He moved to the village in 2020 and was immediately "invited" to join the crew by neighbour Alistair Crowe - who had led the lifeboat appeal.
"It wasn't like there was an option really," recalled Shaw.
"I popped down, had a word with everybody and thought - I'd like to be part of this."
He started out as boat crew and has occupied a number of roles.
"Volunteering, obviously, you get tremendous satisfaction that you are doing a good job and you are there to help people that are in distress," he said.
He said they covered a wide range of callouts and the importance of the service went beyond its work out on the water.
"It isn't all about just going on the boat - it is about supporting our local community as well," he added.
- Published16 June 2020

title: Florovivaismo italiano sul podio mondiale
content:
Il florovivaismo italiano guadagna terreno sui mercati internazionali e consolida il proprio ruolo tra i grandi protagonisti mondiali del settore. A spingere il comparto è soprattutto la domanda estera, con le vendite oltreconfine che continuano a crescere. Secondo i dati Ice elaborati su Trade Data Monitor, nel 2025 le esportazioni di alberi e altre piante vive, bulbi, radici, fiori recisi e fogliame ornamentale hanno raggiunto 1,286 miliardi di euro, il 5,1% in più rispetto agli 1,223 miliardi dell’anno precedente.
Un risultato che mantiene l’Italia sul podio mondiale del settore. Per il triennio 2023-2025 il nostro Paese si conferma infatti terzo esportatore a valore, alle spalle dei Paesi Bassi, principale hub internazionale del commercio florovivaistico, e della Colombia. Nel solo 2025 è aumentato anche il peso dell’Italia sull’export mondiale, con una quota salita dal 4,76 al 4,87%.
A sostenere le vendite sono soprattutto i mercati europei. La Francia resta la prima destinazione dei prodotti italiani, con esportazioni per circa 264,5 milioni di euro, davanti ai Paesi Bassi, con 212,8 milioni, e alla Germania, con 190,6 milioni. Complessivamente questi tre Paesi assorbono più della metà dell’export nazionale, a conferma del forte radicamento del florovivaismo italiano sui principali mercati europei. Per il comparto il 2026 segna anche un passaggio sul fronte normativo. Il decreto legislativo 151, entrato in vigore il 27 agosto, introduce nuove regole per la filiera, intervenendo sulla coltivazione, sulla promozione, sulla commercializzazione e sulla valorizzazione dei prodotti florovivaistici. Un nuovo contesto con cui dovranno confrontarsi imprese e operatori, mentre sostenibilità, innovazione e adattamento ai cambiamenti climatici stanno modificando produzione e gestione del verde.
È in questo scenario che dal 7 al 9 ottobre torna a Fiere di Parma Greenitaly, il Salone internazionale del Florovivaismo e del Paesaggio, giunto alla seconda edizione. L’obiettivo è mettere in relazione la produzione italiana con progettisti, distributori, operatori della gestione del verde e committenza pubblica e privata, rafforzando allo stesso tempo le occasioni di incontro con la domanda internazionale. A Parma sono attesi circa 200 buyer esteri, oltre agli operatori italiani. Le provenienze spaziano dai principali mercati europei – Francia, Germania, Paesi Bassi, Spagna e Regno Unito – al Medio Oriente, con Emirati Arabi Uniti, Arabia Saudita, Qatar e Bahrain, fino a Stati Uniti, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Egitto e Marocco. La composizione degli iscritti restituisce anche la varietà della domanda professionale. Il 42,94% opera nel landscape design, il 14,69% nei garden center e l’8,47% nell’importazione e distribuzione di piante. Gli operatori impegnati nella manutenzione delle aree verdi rappresentano il 3,95%, mentre l’1,69% proviene dalle pubbliche amministrazioni. La restante parte comprende produttori di piante, professionisti del real estate e altri profili legati alla filiera.
Sul fronte dell’offerta, il 54,5% degli espositori italiani arriva dal Nord, il 36,4% dal Centro e il 9,1% dal Sud e dalle Isole. Particolarmente significativa la presenza dell’area vivaistica di Pistoia e della Valdinievole, che rappresenta circa il 24% delle aziende italiane presenti. L’offerta spazia dal vivaismo alla progettazione del paesaggio, fino a vasi, substrati, macchinari e attrezzature.
“Greenitaly si propone come un punto di riferimento internazionale capace di mettere in relazione l’eccellenza del florovivaismo italiano con i principali mercati esteri”, sottolinea Gloria Oppici, brand manager di Greenitaly, Fiere di Parma. “La presenza di buyer e operatori europei ed extraeuropei, insieme a un’offerta espositiva che rappresenta le diverse anime della filiera, conferma la vocazione internazionale del Salone”, prosegue. “A tutto questo si affianca un programma di incontri costruito sui temi che stanno trasformando il settore, dall’innovazione alla sostenibilità, fino alla progettazione e alla gestione del verde. Greenitaly vuole essere il luogo in cui imprese, professionisti e istituzioni possono costruire relazioni, sviluppare nuove opportunità di business e contribuire insieme al futuro del florovivaismo”.
Uno dei temi al centro della manifestazione sarà il rapporto tra verde e città, anche alla luce degli investimenti pubblici degli ultimi anni. Il Pnrr (Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza) ha destinato 210 milioni di euro alla tutela e valorizzazione del verde urbano ed extraurbano e, nell’ultimo trimestre del 2024, è stato raggiunto il target relativo alla messa a dimora di oltre 4,6 milioni di alberi e arbusti attraverso 93 progetti finanziati.
Il programma affronterà così alcune delle questioni che stanno ridisegnando il settore: dal futuro del paesaggio urbano alla ricerca e all’innovazione nella filiera, dalla forestazione al ruolo della natura nella pianificazione delle città. Tra i temi anche la mitigazione degli effetti dei cambiamenti climatici, la sicurezza fitosanitaria delle piante ornamentali, la gestione dell’acqua, del suolo e delle foreste e la valutazione economica e sociale dei servizi ecosistemici prodotti dal verde. Tra gli appuntamenti è previsto il convegno promosso dal Crea, Centro di ricerca Orticoltura e Florovivaismo, dedicato all’innovazione e alla ricerca scientifica applicate al settore, al quale parteciperà Francesco Ferrini, presidente del Distretto Rurale Vivaistico-Ornamentale di Pistoia e professore ordinario di Arboricoltura all’Università degli Studi di Firenze. Ferrini presenterà inoltre a Greenitaly il suo libro dedicato all’arboricoltura urbana.

title: California Tribes receive beach and ancestral village site back from transportation authority
content:
- The U.S. state of California has returned 55 hectares (136 acres) of Northern California coastline, including Blues Beach and the village site of K’etim, to three Coastal Yuki tribes.
- It is the first land Caltrans, the state transportation department, has ever returned to Indigenous ownership.
- Tribes first asked for the site in 2005, after learning looters were digging into archaeological sites and uncovering ancestral remains.
- The tribe hopes to use the land for education and gatherings, but the beach will remain open to the public.
On the Northern California coast, where the tall trees meet the sea, ancestors of the Coast Yuki people lie buried in an old village site above the bluffs in the U.S. state. Yet despite its cultural significance, the land has been owned by the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) until very recently.
A deed recorded July 6 transferred 55 hectares (136 acres) of that coastline to Kai Poma, a nonprofit founded by representatives of the Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians, the Round Valley Indian Tribes and the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians, the Ancestral Descendants of Coastal Yuki and Yuki.
It is the first time land held by Caltrans has been returned to Indigenous ownership, according to Kai Poma.
“We always felt this was ours,” Eddie Knight, chairman of Kai Poma and historic preservation officer for Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians, who is of Coastal Yuki descent, told Mongabay. “It may have been owned privately by somebody, but we still knew it was ours.”
The property sits just south of the small community of Westport, California, about 187 miles (300 kilometers) north of San Francisco. Visitors know the beach here as Blues Beach, but a major village site there is called K’etim by the Coast Yuki and Pomo lineages.
K’etim, according to the tribe’s traditional stories, is “where Seaweed Woman who lived at Mussel Rock met and fell in love with Coyote,” Kai Poma explained in a press release. This origin story “explains the creation of the coastline and its people. These teachings remain alive through the descendants who continue to revere, gather, camp, commune with, and steward their ancestral places.”
In 2005, word reached Knight and others that looters were digging at K’etim and uncovering human and archeological remains. “K’etim has endured substantial damage from off-road vehicle activity and widespread looting of archaeological sites,” Kai Poma stated.
In response, members of Sherwood Valley and Coyote Valley wrote to Caltrans that year asking for stewardship of the site and were granted a meeting. When the land was not handed over, Knight said, “we just kept on being persistent and said ‘give it to us.’”
It took many years of relentless efforts and a new law to make the transfer a reality. In 2021, Senator Mike McGuire wrote Senate Bill 231, specifically authorizing Caltrans to transfer Blues Beach “at no cost to a qualified nonprofit corporation.”
The three tribes formed the non-profit organization Kai Poma to receive the land.
The law requires Kai Poma to keep the land open to the public free of charge, bars commercial development, and returns the land to Caltrans if the nonprofit fails to maintain it or dissolves.
“This is beyond huge,” J. Carlos Rivera, tribal chairman of the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians, told the Los Angeles Times. “It’s enormous from our tribal perspective that we are basically obtaining the land that our people once lived on before colonization.”
The land is made up of about a half mile (800 meters) of beach, a terrace above the beach of roughly 40 hectares (100 acres), “which has our archaeological sites under it,” Knight said, as well as 16 hectares (40 acres) of old grazing land sloping from Highway 1 down to the ocean.
The sloping ground is the part Kai Poma can build on. Future management plans still need to be agreed upon by the three tribes, but Knight raised the possibility of building a traditional roundhouse, holding ceremonies and hosting an educational program.
The beach will remain open to the public. Cars have been prohibited from the beach by Caltrans but that rule was not strictly enforced. Kai Poma is still deciding how they will manage these issues.
“We want to protect the natural habitat,” Knight said. And to educate youth on “how to harvest our native foods, our sea foods, our seaweeds, our kelps and how to fish. Allowing our youth to get an idea of how they can use it in the future and use it now. It’s going to take a little time, but we do have a plan.”
The nonprofit has held a grant since 2023 for an archaeological survey to identify every site on the property, but could not begin the work, Knight said, until they had secured the deed. Now they plan to move forward and are planning a celebration and ceremony for all eight bands in Mendocino County.
This deed transfer is part of a larger Land Back movement: The push to return land to tribes, Traditional Owners and ancestral descendants of the land.
California has returned tens of thousands of acres to tribes in the past two years. The Yurok Tribe reclaimed more than 19,000 hectares (47,000 acres) along the lower Klamath River, the largest land return in state history. The Tule River Indian Tribe regained 6,890 hectares (17,030 acres) in Tulare County, and the Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California reacquired 4,158 hectares (10,274 acres) of former Sierra Nevada ranchland.
“136 acres of coastal lands have now been officially transferred into tribal stewardship, forever protecting one of the most spectacular stretches of the Mendocino Coast,” McGuire said in a statement. “This agreement, the first of its kind in California, gives the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians, Round Valley Indian Tribes and Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians the rightful opportunity to reclaim sacred lands and cultural traditions on this special piece of earth. And it’s about damn time.”

title: Les produits désinfectants ne sont pas toujours utilisés à bon escient : quand sont-ils vraiment nécessaires ?
content:
Les produits désinfectants ne sont pas toujours utilisés à bon escient : quand sont-ils vraiment nécessaires ?
Le SPF Santé publique, sécurité alimentaire et environnement lance une campagne de sensibilisation intitulée "Nettoyez en toute sécurité".
- Publié le 21-09-2026 à 17h50
Les produits désinfectants, oui, mais seulement à bon escient : tel est en quelque sorte le message de la campagne que vient de lancer, pour deux ans, le SPF Santé publique, sécurité alimentaire et environnement en collaboration avec le Centre Antipoisons. Intitulée "Nettoyez en toute sécurité", cette initiative tient à rappeler qu'un produit désinfectant n'est pas indiqué en toutes circonstances, de l'eau et du savon étant généralement suffisants.
C'est que, depuis la crise du Covid, certains ménages belges auraient encore trop souvent tendance à recourir à des produits de nettoyage désinfectants. S'ils s'avèrent utiles dans certaines situations, ils n'apportent aucun bénéfice supplémentaire d'hygiène dans la plupart des cas, alors qu'ils ont un impact négatif sur l'environnement et qu'ils augmentent le risque d'accident.
Jusqu'à la moitié des utilisateurs ne tient pas suffisamment compte du temps de contact (durée pendant laquelle le produit doit agir) ou de la date de péremption, ce qui réduit, voire annule son efficacité. Une utilisation incorrecte ou inutile des produits désinfectants augmente le risque d'accidents", souligne le SPF Santé publique. Ainsi, en 2025, le Centre Antipoisons a reçu 784 appels concernant des accidents impliquant des produits de nettoyage désinfectant. Les produits désinfectants peuvent en effet provoquer de graves irritations de la peau, des yeux et des voies respiratoires.
Règles d'or pour un nettoyage en toute sécurité
À l'adresse des consommateurs, dont les aides-ménagères, cette campagne rappelle les bons réflexes : utiliser le bon produit pour la bonne tâche, lire l'étiquette, aérer pendant le nettoyage, ne jamais mélanger des produits différents, ranger les produits après utilisation et les conserver hors de portée des enfants. "Pour le nettoyage courant, de l'eau et du savon ou un nettoyant multi-usage doux suffisent, précise le SPF. Ils permettent d'éliminer efficacement la saleté, les bactéries et les virus. La désinfection va plus loin : elle détruit presque tous les micro-organismes grâce à des substances chimiques puissantes. Ces produits sont des biocides".
À savoir les situations dans lesquelles la désinfection peut effectivement être recommandée, le SPF cite "en cas de maladie contagieuse à la maison (gastro-entérite, Covid-19 ou infection bactérienne résistante à certains antibiotiques) ; pour protéger une personne immunodéprimée ; après un contact avec des vomissements, du sang ou des selles ; en présence de déjections d'animal sur le sol de la maison ou de moisissures ; et sur avis médical".

title: Portrait : Doumta Jacob, un non-voyant battant
content:
A Sarh, au quartier Baguirmi, dans le 1er arrondissement municipal, Doumta Jacob, un non-voyant, a choisi de faire de son handicap une raison de se battre plutôt qu’un obstacle.
Né à Sarh, chef-lieu de la province du Moyen-Chari, en 1972, Doumta Jacob perd progressivement la vue alors qu’il était encore sur les bancs de l’école. C’est en classe de CM2, à l’âge de 14 ans que ses problèmes de vue ont commencé.
La maladie s’aggrave ensuite et l’oblige à abandonner les études. « Je voyais difficilement le tableau lorsque j’étais à l’ecole et c’était difficile pour moi de lire et d’écrire », raconte-t-il.
Lire aussi : Tchad : une nouvelle association pour l’autonomisation des femmes déficientes visuelles
Contraint de rester à la maison, Doumta Jacob était découragé. Pour l’occuper, sa grand-mère lui remet une somme de 2 000 francs CFA . Avec cet argent, il commence par vendre des cigarettes. Les petits bénéfices réalisés lui permettent ensuite de développer d’autres activités, notamment la vente de bouteilles et la recharge de téléphones portables.
Au fil des années, ces petits commerces lui permettent de construire une chambre et de participer aux dépenses de sa famille. Malgré sa déficience visuelle, il apprend à identifier les différentes pièces et coupures de monnaie, une manière pour lui de s’adapter à son quotidien et à la vente de ses articles.
Lire aussi : Baccalauréat 2025 : cinq candidats déficients visuels composent au sein de l’ONECS
A 53 ans, Doumta Jacob encourage les jeunes à ne pas attendre uniquement un emploi a la Fonction publique. Selon lui, une petite activité peut progressivement devenir une véritable source de revenus.
Son parcours prend une autre dimension lorsqu’il découvre l’écriture braille grâce à un ancien formateur aujourd’hui décédé. « Cette formation m’a permis de lire, d’écrire et de continuer à apprendre malgré mon handicap. Grâce à cette nouvelle forme d’écriture, je compose des chansons. »
La musique devient également une partie importante de sa vie. Dans le monde musical, il se fait appeler Général Litakoï. Comme source d’inspiration, les réalités sociales. Cependant, aucune de ses compositions n’est enregistré au studio, faute de moyens.
« A travers mes chansons, je sensibilise les jeunes sur la consommation excessive de l’alcool, le temps consacré à certaines habitudes qui, selon lui, ne leur apportent pas de bénéfices et la protection de l’environnement. J’ai plusieurs chansons qui sont dans les tiroirs, mais je n’ai pas les moyens de les enregistrer. Je voudrais m’en servir pour sensibiliser les jeunes », explique-t-il.
Doumta Jacob lance également un message aux personnes vivant avec un handicap. Il les invite à identifier leurs capacités et à chercher une activité adaptée à leur situation, plutôt que de rester dans l’attente d’une assistance.
Il plaide enfin pour davantage de possibilités de formation et d’accompagnement en faveur des déficients visuels. Pour lui, un meilleur accès à l’education et aux activités professionnelles pourraient permettre à plusieurs personnes handicapées de devenir davantage autonomes.

title: Hopes new outback museum will spark conversation about town's past
content:
Birdsville's courthouse museum opens after years of planning
In short:
Birdsville's historical courthouse has officially reopened to the public as a museum after two decades of planning.
Current and former residents gathered in town for the opening ceremony.
What's next?
One local family hopes it can spark a conversation about the town's history, particularly its treatment of Indigenous Australians.
Built from local materials on the edge of the Munga-Thirri–Simpson Desert National Park, Birdsville's original courthouse has stood the test of time, through dust storms and droughts, across its century in operation.
The complex was the home of police stationed in the remote outback until it was abandoned in 1988.
Among those helping push for the museum to be created was Maria Sammon Wheeler, who lived in the building as a child when her father was the town officer in the 1960s.
"I really wanted the stories to be told of how life was in those days and to keep them true to form," she said.
"I'm 77 now and [there are] fewer of us to remember accurately.
"It was very harsh on families and wives to live out here under the conditions, but they were amazing conditions for children to grow up in.
However, for other residents, the building also represented a challenging era in town when the government controlled the lives of local Indigenous people.
Sparking a conversation
Wangkangurru man and retiring park ranger Don Rowlands, who has lived in Birdsville all his life, said the building brought up difficult memories for him.
"Growing up … our job was to yard the goats for the police at night and milk them … and deliver the milk to his back door, and more than one time he'd come running out and beat the crap out of us," Mr Rowlands said.
As a child, Mr Rowlands was a ward of the state, which meant local authorities had a significant hand in directing his early years.
"If you wanted your endowment, you had to go to the copper; he was the protector of Aborigines, and he ran all those programs," Mr Rowlands said.
"Sometimes, he'd say yes and sometimes he wouldn't … we just had no control."
Mr Rowlands said he hoped the museum would provide a broader understanding of Birdsville's past.
"It opens a conversation, I guess, for tourists who go through it and come out the other end and then maybe talk to people like myself about the other side of the story," he said.
"It might give it another perspective like we've always been under the thumb."
Elders return to town
Several Indigenous elders also returned for the opening ceremony, some of whom had not been back in almost 30 years.
Mr Rowland's daughter, Peta Rowlands, organised for the elders to come together to celebrate Indigenous history while in town.
"They're all really interested in seeing the school because they've all gone through the state school there," Ms Rowlands said.
"I think there are six kids at the school at the moment and there's only one that's non-Indigenous … it's just another way that we can get the kids to connect with culture and with each other and learn about where they come from.
"I feel like it's a celebration of family coming home; there's always been a want or a desire to come home."
Ms Rowland also believed the museum would allow for further storytelling and reflection.
"Birdsville has changed even in my lifetime; it's changed a lot," she said.
"[Dad] always said to me, 'You've got to make people comfortable to ask the uncomfortable questions.'
"I honestly believe that the more that we talk about it, the more that we acknowledge what happened, whether it was good or bad … I guess that's healing for us as a community to move forward."
Diamantina Shire Mayor Francis Murray said the opening celebrations allowed for everyone to share their views on Birdsville's history.
"I think we've got different versions [of the past], but today, we walked through that door together," Cr Murray said.
"It's an opportunity for everyone to tell their stories."

title: 'Pigs Village' Welsh name change will go ahead
content:
'Pigs Village' Welsh name change will go ahead
- Published
A rural Welsh village will officially change its name to Pentre Moch - literally translated as Pigs Village.
The name dates back to at least the 17th Century and referred to the pig farm around which the Flintshire village of Northop Hall grew.
Northop Hall will retain its English name, but Pentre Moch will become its primary Welsh name following approval by Flintshire council.
The name survived despite restrictions on the Welsh language throughout the 19th Century and will now be added to Ordnance Survey maps, Royal Mail and property records.
There was some opposition, with one resident claiming it would make the village a "laughing stock".
But other residents said the translation did not bother them and was an opportunity for better use of the Welsh language, which they said "isn't heard enough".
Records showed Pentre Moch had been in common use from the 17th Century until restrictions were imposed on the Welsh language in the 19th Century.
As the Welsh language was once more accepted and promoted, Northop Hall became known by the literal translation Neuadd Llaneurgain.
Even then the name endured and a consultation found popular support for the official use of Pentre Moch.
Seconding a motion by councillor Mared Eastwood to approve the adoption of Pentre Moch, councillor Linda Thew said: "Against all the odds, the name Pentre Moch has survived for hundreds of years, passed down from generation to generation to reflect our agricultural past, our ancient woodland where wild boar roamed and were depicted on our heraldic coats of arms.
"This decision will not affect those that wish to use the name Northop Hall. They can continue to use that name, but it will give the opportunity for those who wish to use a Welsh name to do so."
